metric_rationale: This is the empirical effect of the second high-validity cue when the Tallying score is tied. In this fixed design, the two d=0 pairs have feature 0 tied and feature 2 discriminating. Take The Best says feature 2 then breaks the tie, so the B-choice rate should be higher when feature 2 favors B than when feature 2 favors A; in expectation the contrast is (1 - epsilon) * (2 * sigmoid(beta) - 1), where sigmoid(beta) = 1 / (1 + exp(-beta)). Tallying gives feature 2 no special weight; with equal win counts both d=0 cells have choice probability 0.5 under softmax and lapse, so the signed contrast is zero. The per-subject variance is limited because each subject contributes 12 repetitions to each side of the contrast.

This metric is a within-subject first-discriminating-cue contrast: P(choose A | the highest-validity cue that differs favors A) minus P(choose A | it favors B). In this design every trial is exactly tally-balanced, so Tallying predicts P(A)=0.5 in both trial classes and the contrast is 0. Take The Best predicts choices follow the first discriminating cue in validity order, so the A-favoring class should be well above 0.5 and the B-favoring class below 0.5, pushing the contrast toward positive values. Each class contains four unique pairs repeated 12 times, giving stable per-subject proportions.

This metric measures first-cue concordance: for each trial it finds the leftmost displayed feature on which options A and B differ, and codes 1 if the chosen option is the one favored by that feature. Display-order Take The Best predicts high concordance because the first displayed discriminator determines choice, with only weak validity-based modulation. Tallying predicts low concordance in this design: in the eight non-tied pairs the tally favors the opposite option, and in the four tally-balanced pairs it predicts 0.5. Averaging this code over all 96 trials produces a large mean separation and low per-subject variance, so the metric is stable with small human samples.

This metric isolates display-order directional responding on exactly the trials where Tallying has no preference. It selects tally-tie trials, where the feature-wise win counts for A and B are equal. For each first displayed discriminator position, it computes the average B choice rate when the B option is the first discriminator minus the average B choice rate when the A option is the first discriminator, then averages across those positions. Under Tallying, tally ties are uninformative and choice probability is 0.5 in both directions for every position, so this signed difference is close to 0. Under display-order Take The Best, the first discriminator controls choice: B-first trials produce mostly B responses and A-first trials produce mostly A responses. With the design validities 0.53, 0.91, 0.82 and the competing theory's beta/lambda ranges, the per-position differences are approximately 0.4 to 0.9, yielding a pooled value near 0.7. The within-subject signed contrast uses all 30 tally-tie trials per subject, keeping binomial estimation noise small, so the between-theory gap is large relative to between-subject variance.

For each trial, identify the first displayed feature that discriminates between the two options and code whether the response matched the side favored by that discriminating feature. Let c0 be the proportion of position-0 trials with such consistency, and c123 be the mean proportion for positions 1-3. The metric returns c123 - c0. Display-order TTB should produce a positive value because position 0 has low stated validity (0.55), making choices at that position less decisive than at high-validity positions 1-3 (0.85). The primacy-gradient accumulator should produce a negative value because its steep exponential position weights make position 0 dominate despite its lower validity, yielding the highest consistency at position 0 and declining consistency at later positions. This contrast uses both directions of each position and all trials, giving a large mean separation with small per-subject binomial noise.

This metric isolates trials where feature index 1 is the first discriminating feature. Feature 1 has stated validity 0.90, so the display-order TTB theory predicts that it should almost fully determine choice: when A has the high-validity cue, B-response rate is near 0.05; when B has it, B-response rate is near 0.95, producing a difference of roughly -0.90. The advocated capacity-sensitive accumulator has nearly flat weights for 12 features, so the same trials are decided by the accumulated tally. For the A-first index-1 trials the tally is negative or zero and for the B-first index-1 trials it is positive or zero, giving a B-rate difference near +0.59. The two theories therefore produce opposite signs and a large mean separation. Each category contains 24 trials per subject, so the metric also has low per-subject binomial variability.

This metric measures each subject's spread of A-choice frequencies across the eight unique trial types, then averages that within-subject variance. The eight unique trials form four mirror pairs, and every item is exactly balanced at 3 features versus 3 features. The advocated bounded-sampling accumulator has large subject-specific evidence-weight heterogeneity and a steep softmax/lapse transform, so for each mirror pair an individual subject tends to produce one near-impossible A-choice frequency and one near-certain frequency (with lapse, roughly 0.075 and 0.925). Across the eight trial-type frequencies this gives a large and stable within-subject variance (approximately 0.18 in expectation). In contrast, the competing capacity-sensitive accumulator has essentially fixed smooth primacy weights and a common beta, producing only moderate A-choice probabilities across the same eight trial types (approximately 0.23 to 0.77); its within-subject frequency variance is much smaller (approximately 0.04 including binomial noise). Because the metric is computed within subject and then averaged, it is insensitive to subject-level A/B response bias and should separate the two theories strongly with low between-subject variability.

The metric isolates the diagnostic trials in this design where the unweighted tally majority and the early high-validity block point in opposite directions. Every trial has a 4-3 tally margin, and the first three features have validity 0.95 while the last four have validity 0.55. The advocated theory predicts that the capacity collapse makes choices behave like an equal-weight tally, so subjects should choose the option favored by the unweighted tally on these conflict trials at roughly 0.94. The competing theory predicts validity-weighted sampling and a first-cue bonus, so on the same conflict trials subjects should often follow the early high-validity block instead, producing tally agreement around 0.43. The function identifies conflict rows automatically from the feature vectors, then returns the mean response agreement with the tally majority on those rows. Averaging 48 conflict trials per subject keeps the metric tightly estimated while preserving a large expected between-theory gap.

The previous signed slope was near zero under the advocated theory because subjects with partially anti-cue weights produce both positive and negative low-cue slopes, cancelling at the aggregate level. This metric instead measures the magnitude of each subject's sensitivity to the number of low-validity cues opposing the high-validity block. Under the advocated theory, the six low-validity cues systematically influence choice, so the per-subject slope is large in absolute value even when its sign varies. Under the competing theory, normalized high-validity attention dominates and the low-cue balance has little effect, so the absolute slope stays near zero. Averaging per-subject absolute slopes preserves a large between-theory contrast while keeping the metric well-defined for single-subject slices.

This metric combines two per-subject quantities that separate the theories better than the signed low-cue slope alone. First, it estimates the absolute strong-cue orientation effect: the difference in A-choice probability between trials where the position-1 high-validity cue points to A versus B, after controlling for low-cue count. Under the advocated theory the four strong cues are almost balanced and choices stay near chance, so this absolute effect is modest. Under the competing theory subject-level evidence jitter and stochastic sampling break the strong-cue balance, producing large orientation shifts in many subjects; the absolute value is used because the direction is subject-specific. Second, it adds the partial variance explained by the number of low-validity cues favoring A after controlling for strong-cue orientation. This captures the original flat-versus-steep low-count dissociation without being cancelled by sign heterogeneity. The partial effect is multiplied by four to put it on a comparable scale to the orientation effect. Averaging the resulting score across subjects yields a scalar that should be small for the advocated theory and substantially larger for the competing theory.

This metric computes a within-subject contrast between two high-information trial types. For each subject, R_all is the first-cue agreement rate on trials where all four features discriminate, with sign pattern (1,-1,-1,-1) or its mirror (-1,1,1,1). R_near is the first-cue agreement rate on trials where the second displayed feature is tied and only the first cue plus two late cues discriminate, with sign pattern (1,0,-1,-1) or its mirror (-1,0,1,1). The per-subject score is R_near - R_all, and the reported metric is the average of these subject scores.

The contrast isolates the effect of the second cue. In the all-discriminating pattern that cue opposes the first cue, while in the near pattern it is tied. Under the advocated bounded-sampling accumulator, all discriminating cues are sampled at n_features=4 and evidence weights depend on validity rather than serial position, so removing a 0.90-validity opposing cue creates only a modest increase in first-cue choice probability. Under the competing count-sensitive position accumulator, the second displayed position receives a large primacy weight, so removing its opposition should produce a much larger R_near - R_all gap. Thus the two theories predict clearly separated positive values.

Both conditions have 24 trials per subject, the comparison is within-subject, and it avoids the noisy far-tie condition used in the previous failed metric, so between-subject variance should be substantially lower while the mean theory gap remains large.

This metric isolates the core forced-choice conflict in the design. For A-first conflict trials, the first discriminating cue favors A and all later discriminating cues favor B; for mirror trials, the first discriminating cue favors B and all later discriminating cues favor A. Let m_Afirst be the average B-choice rate on A-first conflict trials and m_Bfirst be the average B-choice rate on mirror trials. The metric is m_Bfirst - m_Afirst. The advocated position-weighted accumulator predicts that the later high-validity block outweighs the moderate first cue, so m_Afirst is high, m_Bfirst is low, and the metric is strongly negative. The competing bounded-sampling accumulator predicts first-cue dominance and a large first-cue bonus with no position discounting of the later cues, so m_Afirst is low, m_Bfirst is high, and the metric is positive. Each subject has 48 trials per group because the three conflict pairs and their mirrors are repeated 16 times, which keeps the within-subject aggregate stable.

Targets the only structural disagreement in this design: the adjacent arrangement (discriminating positions 0,1,2) makes the competing model choose the first cue via its odd-one-out bonus, while the advocated model still chooses the two-cue side; in the gap and far arrangements both theories choose the two-cue side. For each trial I locate the leftmost discriminating cue, code whether the response followed that cue, and contrast the adjacent first-cue rate against the pooled gap/far first-cue rate. Under the advocated model the first-cue rate is the same across arrangements because all three discriminating cues are sampled and positional effects are negligible, so this contrast is near zero for every subject (tight variance). Under the competing model the adjacent arrangement has a large first-cue advantage, so the contrast is strongly positive. The metric uses 32 adjacent and 64 baseline trials per subject, keeping per-subject binomial noise small.

Leftmost-discriminating-cue adherence directly probes the first-cue bonus that separates the two accounts. In this fixed design the first three display positions are tied on every trial, so the first discriminating cue is always the high-validity tail cue at position 3 except in the two single-position-4 pairs. The advocated model places positions 3 and 4 in a weak tail with only a tiny recency edge at n=5, giving near-chance conflict trials and only moderate single/same-direction choices, so pooled adherence is expected near 0.59. The bounded-sampling model has capacity (5/5)^0.5 = 1 at n=5, samples every discriminating cue, and adds an unattenuated first-cue bonus, yielding adherence near 0.84-0.92 and a pooled value near 0.89. Averaging over all 96 trials per subject yields a large mean gap with small within-subject binomial variance, making the metric reliably discriminable for 25 subjects.

The metric isolates the high-density adjacent configural odd-one-out trial type: first discriminating cue at position 0, with two opposing cues immediately at positions 1 and 2. In this focal type the competing theory's large odd-one-out bonus strongly favors the first cue, whereas the advocated theory gives little or no first-cue advantage. Subtracting the average first-cue matching rate in the remaining configural trials removes each subject's general bias and scale effects, producing a tight between-subject contrast while retaining a large between-theory difference.

After the first two trials, all past histories contain only late-first-cue trials, so the competing model's tie-run reset is active and turns single-cue evidence negative: it predicts below-chance choice of the cue-bearing option. The advocated model has no history dependence and accumulates the late cue positively via its recency-weighted tail, predicting above-chance cue choice. This metric uses each subject's third trial onward, selects exactly one-discriminating-cue trials with the cue at position 3 or later, and returns the proportion choosing the cue-bearing option. The eight unique pairs are repeated 12 times, so the per-subject proportion is stable, and pooled and per-subject estimates align.

At n=8 the two theories differ most in the sign of mid_early_polarity: the advocated theory has a positive early polarity while the competing theory has a negative early polarity. In this design all discriminating cues are inside the early span and the tail is tied, so the first cue's sign propagates through the early block. On trials where the first two discriminating cues agree, the advocated theory should choose the product favored by those first cues, while the competing theory should reverse that early evidence and choose the opposite product. The metric therefore scores each qualifying trial as +1 when the response matches the first cue and -1 otherwise, then averages. It excludes the mixed + - + trials whose early evidence is near boundary and could be noisy. This gives a stable scalar near +1 under the advocated theory and near -1 under the competing theory.

Every trial in this design has exactly two discriminating cues: an early first cue at position 0, 1, or 2 followed by a tie gap, and one opposing low-validity tail cue at position 4. The advocated theory applies a tie-gap penalty to the first cue on these non-configural single-opposing-cue displays, shrinking it so much that at position 2 the tail cue can reverse the first-cue direction and overall first-cue following stays near chance. The competing theory does not apply a tie-gap penalty here, so its strong early block keeps first-cue following clearly above chance at every position. The metric therefore pools all 96 trials per subject, balanced across A-first and B-first mirror pairs, and returns the excess rate of choosing the option favored by the first discriminating cue over chance. This should be near zero or slightly negative under the advocated theory and strongly positive under the competing theory, with low per-subject variance because it averages many binary responses.

On every trial the first two discriminating cues point to the same option and exactly one later cue points the opposite way. The advocated model heavily discounts the n=10 first-position cue and nearly erases the same-run position-1 cue, so the lone later opposing cue drives choice; the competing model gives the first two same-direction cues a strong same-run boost and therefore produces more early-consistent choices. Computing the empirical log-odds of choosing the option favored by the first two discriminating cues converts this dissociation into a sign contrast: advocated data should sit below zero and competing data near or above zero. Each subject contributes 96 randomized trials, so the per-subject estimate is stable and the metric remains tight across subjects.

This metric isolates the two-cue early-block condition, where the first two discriminating cues favor the same option and the next position is tied before four high-validity tail cues oppose them. It returns the proportion of trials on which the subject chose the option favored by that two-cue early run. Under the advocated theory, subjects mix a zero-early branch with a moderately positive branch; the zero branch follows the strong tail and the positive branch is only weakly early-favoring, so the proportion sits near chance around 0.4-0.6. Under the competing theory, nearly all subjects have a large positive n=7 early polarity, so the same two weak early cues dominate the high-validity tail and the proportion remains near ceiling around 0.90. Mirrored trials are included and the early-choice indicator is sign-adjusted, so option bias cancels. There are 48 trials per subject in this condition, giving a stable per-subject value.
